subject: math
title: Measuring Angles: Degrees, Protractors and Unknown Angles
seo_title: Grade 4 Measuring Angles Worksheets: Protractor, Degrees, Acute and Obtuse, Unknown Angles
standard_text: Recognize angles as geometric shapes that are formed wherever two rays share a common endpoint, and understand concepts of angle measurement: an angle that turns through 1/360 of a circle is a one-degree angle. Measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor. Sketch angles of specified measure. Recognize angle measure as additive. Solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram in real world and mathematical problems.
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 angle worksheets: angles as turns and degrees, reading the inner and outer scales of a protractor, acute, right, obtuse and straight angles, adding angles, and finding unknown angles in word problems. 100 practice questions with answers.
key_big: An angle measures a turn. A full turn is 360°, a quarter turn is 90°.
key_sub: On a protractor, put the center on the vertex, line up one ray with 0, and read the scale that starts at that 0. Angle parts add up: on a straight line to 180°, around a point to 360°.
body_html:
An angle is a turn

An angle is made by two rays that start at the same point, the vertex. Its size is how far one ray turns to reach the other. We measure that turn in degrees (°). A full turn is 360°, so 1° is 1360 of a circle.

Measure with a protractor

1. Put the center mark on the vertex. 2. Line up one ray with 0. 3. Read the scale that starts at 0 on that ray, where the other ray crosses it. 4. Check: is the angle smaller or bigger than a right angle?

Kinds of angles

KindSizeExample
Acuteless than 90°30°, 75°
Rightexactly 90° (square corner)corner of a book
Obtusemore than 90°, less than 180°120°, 145°
Straightexactly 180°a straight line

Angle measures add

When an angle is split into parts that do not overlap, the parts add up to the whole angle. So you can add to find the whole, or subtract to find a missing part.

Missing part

Angle ABC is 120°. One part is 75°. What is the other part?

The parts add up to 120°: 75° + ? = 120°. Subtract: 120° − 75° = 45°.

Answer: 45°

The angles make…They add up to
a right angle90°
a straight line180°
a full turn around a point360°

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Reading the wrong scale (130° for a 50° angle)Read the scale that starts at 0 on your ray, then check: small or big angle?
Counting each small mark as 1° (61° instead of 65°)Check what the marks count by. On this protractor they go by 5s
Not putting the center mark on the vertexPut the center mark exactly on the vertex before you read
Using 180° when the angles make a right angle or a full turnRight angle: 90°. Straight line: 180°. All the way around: 360°
Adding when a part is missingIf you know the whole, subtract the known part

faq.q: How do you teach measuring angles in 4th grade?
faq.a: Start with turns: a quarter turn is 90° and a full turn is 360°. Then use a protractor: center mark on the vertex, one ray on 0, and read the scale that starts at that 0.

faq.q: Which number do you read on a protractor, the inner or the outer?
faq.a: Read the scale that has 0 on the ray you lined up. Then check: if the angle is smaller than a right angle, the answer must be less than 90°.

faq.q: What does it mean that angle measure is additive?
faq.a: If an angle is split into parts that do not overlap, the parts add up to the whole. For example, 40° + 35° = 75°, so a missing part can be found by subtracting.

They are the Common Core Grade 4 standards on angles: understand degrees as parts of a 360° turn, measure and sketch angles with a protractor, and add and subtract angle measures to find unknown angles.

sets.title: Angles as turns: degrees, quarter turns and clocks

items.q: The red ray turned from the green ray. How many degrees is this turn?
items.e: A full turn is 360°. A 1/4 turn is one of 4 equal parts: 90°. It makes a right angle. (25° would be true only if a circle had 100 degrees.)

items.q: What fraction of a full turn is 1°?
items.e: A full turn is 360 one-degree angles, so 1° is 1360 of a turn.

items.q: A clock face is a full turn split into 12 equal hour spaces. How many degrees is each hour space?
items.e: 360° ÷ 12 = 30°. (5 is the number of minutes in each hour space, not the degrees.)

items.q: An angle that turns through 1360 of a circle measures ___.
items.e: A circle is cut into 360 tiny equal turns. Each one is 1 degree (1°).

items.q: What is the measure of the shaded angle between the clock hands?
items.e: Each hour space is 30° (360° ÷ 12). From 12 to 2 is 2 hour spaces: 30° + 30° = 60°.

items.q: The ray turned all the way around. How many degrees is that?
items.e: A full turn goes all the way around and comes back to the start: 360°.

items.q: What fraction of a full turn is 90°?
items.e: 90° + 90° + 90° + 90° = 360°, so 90° is 1 of 4 equal parts: a 1/4 turn.

items.q: What is the measure of the shaded angle between the clock hands?
items.e: Each hour space is 30° (360° ÷ 12). From 12 to 4 is 4 hour spaces: 4 × 30° = 120°.

items.q: How many degrees are in a full turn (a whole circle)?
items.e: A full turn is 360°. Half a turn is 180° and a quarter turn is 90°.

items.q: The minute hand moves from 12 to 9, the long way round (clockwise). How many degrees does it turn?
items.e: 12 to 3, 3 to 6 and 6 to 9 are three quarter turns: 3 × 90° = 270°. (90° is the short way back from 9 to 12.)

items.q: How many 1/4 turns make a full turn?
An angle turns through 140 one-degree angles. What is its measure?
items.e: Each one-degree angle adds 1°: 140 of them make 140°.

items.q: An angle turns through 75 one-degree angles. What is its measure?
items.e: 75 one-degree angles make 75°. (76° comes from counting the marks instead of the spaces between them.)

items.q: What is the measure of the shaded angle between the clock hands?
items.e: Each hour space is 30° (360° ÷ 12). From 12 to 6 is 6 hour spaces: 6 × 30° = 180°. That is a 1/2 turn, a straight angle.

items.q: What is the measure of the shaded angle between the clock hands?
items.e: Each hour space is 30° (360° ÷ 12). From 12 to 1 is 1 hour space: 30°.

items.q: What fraction of a full turn is 180°?
items.e: 180° is half of 360°, so it is a 1/2 turn.

items.q: How many degrees is the turn shown?
items.e: A 1/2 turn is half of 360°: 180°. The two rays point in opposite directions and make a straight line.

items.q: What is the measure of the shaded angle between the clock hands?
items.e: Each hour space is 30° (360° ÷ 12). From 12 to 3 is 3 hour spaces: 30° + 30° + 30° = 90°. That is a 1/4 turn, a right angle.

items.q: What is the measure of the shaded angle between the clock hands?
items.e: Each hour space is 30° (360° ÷ 12). From 12 to 5 is 5 hour spaces: 5 × 30° = 150°.

items.q: The ray turned 3 quarter turns. How many degrees is that?
items.e: A 3/4 turn is 3 quarter turns: 90° + 90° + 90° = 270°.

sets.title: Read a protractor: inner and outer scales

items.q: What is the measure of the angle?
items.e: The bottom ray points to 0 on the right, so read the inner scale, which starts at 0 on the right. The other ray crosses it at 30°. The outer scale says 150 there, but that scale starts from the other side. The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 30° makes sense.

items.q: Neither ray is on 0. What is the measure of the angle?
items.e: On the inner scale one ray is at 20 and the other is at 75. The angle is the difference: 75° − 20° = 55°.

items.q: Neither ray is on 0. What is the measure of the angle?
items.e: On the inner scale one ray is at 30 and the other is at 110. The angle is the difference: 110° − 30° = 80°.

items.q: What is the measure of the angle?
items.e: The bottom ray points to 0 on the right, so read the inner scale, which starts at 0 on the right. The other ray crosses it at 145°. The marks go by 5s, so the mark between 140 and 150 is 145. The outer scale says 35 there, but that scale starts from the other side. The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 145° makes sense.

items.q: What is the measure of the angle?
items.e: The bottom ray points to 0 on the right, so read the inner scale, which starts at 0 on the right. The other ray crosses it at 120°. The outer scale says 60 there, but that scale starts from the other side. The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 120° makes sense.

items.q: What is the measure of the angle?
items.e: The bottom ray points to 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other ray crosses it at 50°. (The inner scale says 130 there.) The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 50° makes sense.

items.q: What is the measure of the angle?

items.q: What is the measure of the angle?
items.e: The bottom ray points to 0 on the right, so read the inner scale, which starts at 0 on the right. The other ray crosses it at 65°. The marks go by 5s, so the mark between 60 and 70 is 65. The outer scale says 115 there, but that scale starts from the other side. The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 65° makes sense.

items.q: Where do you put the center mark of a protractor when you measure an angle?
c: in the middle of a ray
at the end of a ray
items.e: The center mark goes on the vertex, the point where the two rays meet. Then line up one ray with 0.

items.q: What is the measure of the angle?
items.e: The bottom ray points to 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other ray crosses it at 25°. The marks go by 5s, so the mark between 20 and 30 is 25. (The inner scale says 155 there.) The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 25° makes sense.

items.q: What is the measure of the angle?
items.e: The bottom ray points to 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other ray crosses it at 115°. The marks go by 5s, so the mark between 110 and 120 is 115. (The inner scale says 65 there.) The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 115° makes sense.

items.q: What is the measure of the angle?
items.e: The bottom ray points to 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other ray crosses it at 40°. (The inner scale says 140 there.) The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 40° makes sense.

items.q: What is the measure of the angle?
items.e: The bottom ray points to 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other ray crosses it at 135°. The marks go by 5s, so the mark between 130 and 140 is 135. (The inner scale says 45 there.) The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 135° makes sense.

items.q: What is the measure of the angle?
items.e: The bottom ray points to 0 on the right, so read the inner scale, which starts at 0 on the right. The other ray crosses it at 80°. The outer scale says 100 there, but that scale starts from the other side. The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 80° makes sense.

items.q: One ray of an angle is on the 0 of the outer scale. Which numbers should you read?
items.e: Read the scale that starts at 0 on your ray. Here that is the outer scale.

items.q: Neither ray is on 0. What is the measure of the angle?
items.e: On the inner scale one ray is at 60 and the other is at 150. The angle is the difference: 150° − 60° = 90°.

items.q: Ana measures an angle that is clearly wider than a right angle. Her protractor shows 55 and 125 where the ray crosses. What is the angle?
items.e: An angle wider than a right angle is more than 90°, so it is 125°. 55° is the reading on the wrong scale.

items.q: What is the measure of the angle?
items.e: The bottom ray points to 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other ray crosses it at 75°. The marks go by 5s, so the mark between 70 and 80 is 75. (The inner scale says 105 there.) The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 75° makes sense.

items.q: What is the measure of the angle?
items.e: The bottom ray points to 0 on the right, so read the inner scale, which starts at 0 on the right. The other ray crosses it at 160°. The outer scale says 20 there, but that scale starts from the other side. The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 160° makes sense.

items.q: What is the measure of the angle?
items.e: The bottom ray points to 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other ray crosses it at 100°. (The inner scale says 80 there.) The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 100° makes sense.

sets.title: Acute, right, obtuse and straight: name and estimate

items.q: Which is the best estimate for this angle?
items.e: Compare with a right angle (90°). This angle is smaller than a right angle, so about 60° fits. (It is 62°.) About 120° is wider than a right angle, so it cannot be the answer.

items.q: Which is the best estimate for this angle?
items.e: The rays almost make a straight line (180°), so it is about 180°. (It is 170°.) About 10° is a tiny angle, almost closed.

items.q: Which angle measure is acute?
items.e: Acute means less than 90°. Only 75° is less than 90°.

items.q: What kind of angle is this?
items.e: A right angle is exactly 90°, a square corner. The small square shows it. This angle is 90°. Turning an angle does not change its size.

items.q: An angle measures 135°. What kind of angle is it?
items.e: 135° is more than 90° and less than 180°, so it is obtuse.

items.q: Which is the best estimate for this angle?
items.e: Compare with a right angle (90°). This angle is smaller than a right angle, so about 30° fits. (It is 28°.) About 150° is wider than a right angle, so it cannot be the answer.

items.q: Omar says a 100° angle is acute because 100 is a small number. Is he right?
items.e: 100° is more than 90°, so the angle is wider than a right angle. That makes it obtuse.

items.q: What kind of angle is this?
items.e: An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle: between 90° and 180°. This angle is 120°.

items.q: An angle measures 180°. What kind of angle is it?
items.e: 180° is a half turn. The rays make a straight line, so it is a straight angle.

items.q: What kind of angle is this?
items.e: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle: less than 90°. This angle is 60°.

items.q: What kind of angle is this?
items.e: A straight angle is 180°. The two rays point in opposite directions and make a straight line. This angle is 180°.

items.q: What kind of angle is this?
items.e: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle: less than 90°. This angle is 30°.

items.q: Which is the best estimate for this angle?
items.e: Compare with a right angle (90°). This angle is bigger than a right angle but not close to a straight line, so about 120° fits. (It is 122°.) About 60° is smaller than a right angle, so it cannot be the answer.

items.q: Which is the best estimate for this angle?
items.e: Compare with a right angle (90°). This angle is smaller than a right angle, so about 45° fits. (It is 47°.) About 135° is wider than a right angle, so it cannot be the answer.

items.q: Which is the best estimate for this angle?
items.e: Compare with a right angle (90°). This angle is bigger than a right angle, so about 150° fits. (It is 148°.) About 30° is smaller than a right angle, so it cannot be the answer.

items.q: What kind of angle is this?
items.e: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle: less than 90°. This angle is 20°.

items.q: What kind of angle is this?
items.e: An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle: between 90° and 180°. This angle is 145°.

items.q: What kind of angle is this?
items.e: A right angle is exactly 90°, a square corner. The small square shows it. This angle is 90°.

items.q: Which could be the measure of an obtuse angle?
items.e: An obtuse angle is between 90° and 180°. 140° is the only one in that range.

items.q: How many right angles make a straight angle?
items.e: 90° + 90° = 180°, so 2 right angles make a straight angle. (4 right angles make a full turn.)

items.q: Two angles of 45° are put side by side with no gap and no overlap. What angle do they make together?
items.e: Angle measures add: 45° + 45° = 90°. Together they make a right angle.

items.q: The angle is split into 4 equal parts. One part is 30°. What is the whole angle?
items.e: There are 4 equal parts (count the spaces between the rays, not the rays). 4 × 30° = 120°.

items.q: The angle is split into 3 equal parts. One part is 25°. What is the whole angle?
items.e: There are 3 equal parts (count the spaces between the rays, not the rays). 3 × 25° = 75°.

items.q: Angle ABC measures 135°. What is the measure of angle DBC?
items.e: The two parts add up to the whole: 90° + ? = 135°. Subtract: 135° − 90° = 45°. Check: 90° + 45° = 135°.

items.q: Angle ABC is split into two angles by ray BD. What is the measure of angle ABC?
items.e: Angle measures add: 70° + 50° = 120°. The two parts share ray BD and do not overlap, so together they make angle ABC.

items.q: Angle ABC measures 150°. What is the measure of angle DBC?
items.e: The two parts add up to the whole: 65° + ? = 150°. Subtract: 150° − 65° = 85°. Check: 65° + 85° = 150°.

items.q: Angle ABC is split into two angles by ray BD. What is the measure of angle ABC?
items.e: Angle measures add: 55° + 45° = 100°. The two parts share ray BD and do not overlap, so together they make angle ABC. Remember to regroup: 5 + 5 = 10.

items.q: Angle ABC measures 100°. What is the measure of angle DBC?
items.e: The two parts add up to the whole: 45° + ? = 100°. Subtract: 100° − 45° = 55°. Check: 45° + 55° = 100°.

items.q: Angle ABC is split into two angles by ray BD. What is the measure of angle ABC?
items.e: Angle measures add: 110° + 30° = 140°. The two parts share ray BD and do not overlap, so together they make angle ABC.

items.q: Angle ABC is split into two angles by ray BD. What is the measure of angle ABC?
items.e: Angle measures add: 90° + 45° = 135°. The two parts share ray BD and do not overlap, so together they make angle ABC.

items.q: Angle ABC is split into two angles by ray BD. What is the measure of angle ABC?
items.e: Angle measures add: 25° + 60° = 85°. The two parts share ray BD and do not overlap, so together they make angle ABC.

items.q: Angle ABC measures 115°. What is the measure of angle DBC?
items.e: The two parts add up to the whole: 70° + ? = 115°. Subtract: 115° − 70° = 45°. Check: 70° + 45° = 115°.

items.q: Angle ABC measures 80°. What is the measure of angle DBC?
items.e: The two parts add up to the whole: 35° + ? = 80°. Subtract: 80° − 35° = 45°. Check: 35° + 45° = 80°.

items.q: Angle ABC measures 125°. What is the measure of angle DBC?
items.e: The two parts add up to the whole: 50° + ? = 125°. Subtract: 125° − 50° = 75°. Check: 50° + 75° = 125°.

items.q: Angle ABC measures 160°. What is the measure of angle DBC?
items.e: The two parts add up to the whole: 25° + ? = 160°. Subtract: 160° − 25° = 135°. Check: 25° + 135° = 160°.

items.q: Angle PQR is 120°. Ray QS splits it into two angles. One of them is 75°. What is the other?
items.e: The two parts add up to 120°. 120° − 75° = 45°. Check: 75° + 45° = 120°.

items.q: Angle ABC measures 95°. What is the measure of angle DBC?
items.e: The two parts add up to the whole: 40° + ? = 95°. Subtract: 95° − 40° = 55°. Check: 40° + 55° = 95°.

items.q: Angle ABC is split into two angles by ray BD. What is the measure of angle ABC?
items.e: Angle measures add: 65° + 75° = 140°. The two parts share ray BD and do not overlap, so together they make angle ABC. Remember to regroup: 5 + 5 = 10.

items.q: Angle ABC is split into two angles by ray BD. What is the measure of angle ABC?
items.e: Angle measures add: 40° + 35° = 75°. The two parts share ray BD and do not overlap, so together they make angle ABC.

items.q: Angle ABC is split into two angles by ray BD. What is the measure of angle ABC?
items.e: Angle measures add: 35° + 85° = 120°. The two parts share ray BD and do not overlap, so together they make angle ABC. Remember to regroup: 5 + 5 = 10.

items.q: The whole angle is a right angle. What is the unknown angle?
items.e: A right angle is 90°. 90° − 35° = 55°. (Using 180° would give 145°, but this is a right angle, not a straight line.)

items.q: Three roads meet at one point. Two of the angles between them are 120° and 135°. What is the third angle?
items.e: The three angles go all the way around the point: 360°. 120° + 135° = 255°, and 360° − 255° = 105°.

items.q: Emma rides a skateboard. She turns 90°, then turns 180° more in the same direction. How many degrees does she turn in all?
items.e: Turns in the same direction add: 90° + 180° = 270°. That is a 3/4 turn.

items.q: The two angles sit on a straight line. What is the unknown angle?
items.e: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. 180° − 125° = 55°. Check: 125° + 55° = 180°.

items.q: A lawn sprinkler sprays water through 60°, then through 70° more. How many more degrees must it turn to make a full turn?
items.e: So far: 60° + 70° = 130°. A full turn is 360°: 360° − 130° = 230°. (Using 180° would give 50°.)

items.q: Three angles go all the way around a point. What is the unknown angle?
items.e: Angles all the way around a point add up to 360°, a full turn. 120° + 150° = 270°, and 360° − 270° = 90°.

items.q: A skate ramp meets the flat ground at a 25° angle. What is the angle between the ramp and the ground on the other side?
items.e: The ground is a straight line, so the two angles add up to 180°. 180° − 25° = 155°.

items.q: Three angles go all the way around a point. What is the unknown angle?
items.e: Angles all the way around a point add up to 360°, a full turn. 90° + 160° = 250°, and 360° − 250° = 110°.

items.q: At 3:00 the hands of a clock make a right angle. What angle do they make at 4:00?
items.e: Each hour space is 30°. At 4:00 the hour hand is 4 spaces from 12: 4 × 30° = 120°. That is 90° + 30°.

items.q: The two angles sit on a straight line. What is the unknown angle?
items.e: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. 180° − 70° = 110°. Check: 70° + 110° = 180°.

items.q: A round pizza is cut into 4 equal slices from the center. What angle does each slice make at the center?
items.e: The slices go all the way around the center: 360°. 360° ÷ 4 = 90°. (Using 180° would give 45°.)

items.q: The minute hand of a clock moves for 20 minutes. How many degrees does it turn?
items.e: Every 5 minutes is one hour space, which is 30°. 20 minutes is 4 spaces: 4 × 30° = 120°.

items.q: Noah opens a pair of scissors to 45°. Then he opens them 35° more. What is the angle now?
items.e: Opening more makes the angle bigger: 45° + 35° = 80°. (Remember to regroup: 5 + 5 = 10.)

items.q: The whole angle is a right angle. What is the unknown angle?
items.e: A right angle is 90°. 90° − 60° = 30°. (Using 180° would give 120°, but this is a right angle, not a straight line.)

items.q: A laptop screen is open at 110°. Nora pushes it back 15° more. What angle is the screen open at now?
items.e: Pushing the screen back opens it more: 110° + 15° = 125°.

items.q: A pie is cut into 6 equal slices. Each slice makes a 60° angle at the center. Ava eats 2 slices. What angle do the slices that are left make?
items.e: The whole pie is 360°. 2 slices are 2 × 60° = 120°. 360° − 120° = 240°. (Or 4 slices are left: 4 × 60° = 240°.)

items.q: The two angles sit on a straight line. What is the unknown angle?
items.e: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. 180° − 40° = 140°. Check: 40° + 140° = 180°.

items.q: Jack opens a door until it makes a right angle with the wall. Then he closes it by 35°. What angle does the door make with the wall now?
items.e: A right angle is 90°. Closing the door makes the angle smaller: 90° − 35° = 55°.

items.q: The whole angle is a right angle. What is the unknown angle?
items.e: A right angle is 90°. 90° − 25° = 65°. (Using 180° would give 155°, but this is a right angle, not a straight line.)

items.q: Three angles go all the way around a point. What is the unknown angle?
items.e: Angles all the way around a point add up to 360°, a full turn. 100° + 135° = 235°, and 360° − 235° = 125°.
